claims.text: Tailored annealing and cooling can direct phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
The targeted phase evolution produces a fine-scale lamellar microstructure with alternating ordered and disordered phases.
The as-cast Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA has a coarse, inhomogeneous phase distribution.
An effective treatment window is approximately 900–1200 °C near the eutectic temperature.
Annealing for 1–2 hours is an appropriate duration for controlling phase evolution.
Prescribed cooling can balance diffusion-driven ordering with retention of a disordered matrix.
The structural mediator is a population of nanoscale ordered precipitates, such as B2, embedded in a continuous disordered matrix.
Annealing increases atomic mobility and thereby enables nucleation and growth of ordered phases.
Cooling rate controls the size and dispersion of ordered regions.
Changing the size and dispersion of ordered regions adjusts interphase spacing.
Interphase spacing influences the mechanical response.
The refined lamellar microstructure should improve the strength–ductility balance relative to the as-cast state.
The as-cast alloy has suboptimal mechanical properties.
Large deviations from the proposed processing window may cause phase overgrowth or formation of undesirable phases.
Phase stability and transformation kinetics may vary with composition.

contradictions.description: The mediator is described as discrete nanoscale precipitates embedded in a continuous matrix, whereas the predicted outcome is an alternating lamellar two-phase morphology; the relationship between these distinct morphologies is not explained.

The hypothesis describes the as-cast state as coarse, poorly controlled, and mechanically suboptimal, but the cited same-system record reports an as-cast fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure with approximately 2 µm spacing, 944 MPa fracture stress, and 25.6% elongation.
